name: Postpartum Mood Disorders
preview_text: Not all postpartum depression is the same. The tight-chested irritability of Liver Qi Stagnation, the exhausted emptiness of Heart and Spleen Deficiency, and the foggy heaviness of...
conventional_description: Postpartum depression is a mood disorder that can affect women after childbirth, marked by persistent sadness, anxiety, exhaustion, and difficulty bonding with the baby. It's more severe and longer-lasting than the "baby blues," which typically resolve within two weeks. Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, and it affects roughly 10-15% of new mothers.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment includes psychotherapy, especially cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and antidepressant medications such as SSRIs. Support groups and lifestyle adjustments are also recommended. For severe cases, newer options like brexanolone may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, postpartum depression is understood as a profound disruption of the body's Qi and Blood following childbirth. Delivery involves significant blood loss and a massive expenditure of Qi, leaving the body temporarily empty. The Liver, which stores Blood and ensures the smooth flow of Qi, is particularly vulnerable. When Liver Blood is depleted, Liver Qi easily stagnates, producing the irritability, frustration, and chest tightness so common in new mothers. This is the Liver Qi Stagnation pattern - the most frequent TCM diagnosis for postpartum depression.
But the Liver is only part of the story. The Spleen, which transforms food into Qi and Blood, is often weakened by the physical demands of pregnancy and delivery. When the Spleen cannot replenish what was lost, both Qi and Blood become deficient. The Heart, which relies on Blood to anchor the mind (Shen), becomes undernourished, leading to the emotional fragility, palpitations, and insomnia of Heart and Spleen Deficiency. In other cases, stagnant Qi combines with Spleen-generated dampness to form Phlegm, which clouds the mind and creates a heavy, foggy depression with a sensation of a lump in the throat. And when blood loss is severe, or if cold enters the body postpartum, Blood Stagnation can develop, causing a depression that feels physically stuck, with stabbing pains and dark lochia.
This is why TCM doesn't treat all postpartum depression the same way. The mother who sighs constantly, snaps at her partner, and feels a knot in her chest needs Liver Qi soothed. The mother who can barely get out of bed, has no appetite, and feels her heart racing needs Spleen and Heart nourished. The mother with mental fog and a lump in her throat needs Phlegm resolved. Each pattern has its own treatment, and often a woman will have a mix - which is why a skilled practitioner's pattern differentiation is so important.
classical_quote: 「产后血气俱虚，心神不守，故令悲喜无常，或歌哭嗔怒。」
classical_translation: "After childbirth, both blood and qi are deficient, the heart spirit is not secured, therefore causing unpredictable sadness and joy, or singing, crying, and anger."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 43, Postpartum Depression 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening carefully to how the low mood actually feels and what other signs accompany it. They will ask about your emotional triggers, your energy level, your appetite, and the quality of your sleep - because the combination of these clues is what separates one pattern from another. The tongue and pulse are then checked to confirm the picture.
If the main complaint is a tight, frustrated feeling in the chest, frequent sighing, and irritability that flares with stress, the practitioner suspects Liver Qi Stagnation. The tongue often looks normal or slightly purplish with a thin white coat, and the pulse feels wiry, like a guitar string. This is the most common pattern after childbirth.
When exhaustion, poor appetite, loose stools, and a pale face join the low mood - along with heart palpitations and restless sleep - the focus shifts to Heart and Spleen Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is thin and weak. This pattern reflects the heavy toll of blood loss and physical depletion on both the digestive system and the mind.
Sometimes a person describes a sensation of something stuck in the throat, a foggy head, and a heavy, oppressed chest. That points toward Qi-Phlegm, a less common pattern where stagnant Qi and fluids combine into a thick, obstructive substance. The tongue appears puffy with a greasy white coating, and the pulse feels slippery or rolling.
If the depression is accompanied by fixed, stabbing pains - especially in the lower abdomen - and the lochia has been dark or clotted, Blood Stagnation is likely. The tongue looks purplish with stasis spots, and the pulse is choppy or wiry. A similar but milder pattern is Heart Blood Deficiency alone, where emotional fragility, dizziness, and poor memory dominate, but digestive symptoms are absent; the tongue is pale and thin, and the pulse is fine.

patterns.symptoms: ["Frequent sighing and a sensation of a lump in the throat", "Irritability and mood swings that worsen with stress", "Distension and tightness in the chest and rib area", "Breast tenderness or swelling"]
patterns.worse_with: Stress and frustration, Suppressing emotions, Fatty, greasy foods, Lack of sleep, Feeling isolated or unsupported
patterns.better_with: Gentle walking or stretching, Warm peppermint tea, Talking about feelings, A calm, supportive environment
patterns.why_this_happens: After childbirth, blood loss and the demands of caring for a newborn can leave the Liver’s Blood depleted, making it more vulnerable to stagnation. When Liver Qi gets stuck, it fails to spread smoothly through the chest and ribs, producing the hallmark feelings of frustration, frequent sighing, and a tight, distended sensation. This stuck energy can then rise to disturb the mind, leading to irritability, tearfulness, and a low mood that feels like a knot that won’t loosen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body, red or slightly purple sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), taut like a guitar string, most noticeable at the left middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and emotional suppression directly aggravate Liver Qi stagnation, causing the tight, stuck sensation to intensify. Gentle movement and stretching physically unblock the flow of Qi through the channels, while warm, aromatic teas like peppermint have a dispersing nature that helps move stagnant energy. Talking through emotions and resting in a calm space prevents Qi from knotting up, allowing the Liver to regain its smooth, free-flowing function.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Gentle daily movement like walking or postnatal yoga helps keep Qi flowing. Sip warm peppermint or chrysanthemum tea, and favour light, easily digestible meals with leafy greens. Create space to talk about your feelings with a trusted friend, and avoid suppressing emotions.

patterns.why_this_happens: Childbirth involves significant blood loss and intense physical effort, which directly depletes the body's Qi and Blood. The Spleen, which produces Qi and Blood, becomes too weak to replenish what was lost, while the Heart Blood that anchors the mind runs low. This dual deficiency leaves you profoundly exhausted, unable to digest food properly, and mentally restless - the mind lacks the nourishment to stay calm, leading to insomnia, palpitations, and a low, foggy mood.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and teeth-marked with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine and weak, especially empty at the left Cun (Heart) position and soft at the right Guan (Spleen) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen is the source of Qi and Blood; overwork, worry, and poor diet weaken it further, while cold foods dampen its digestive fire. Rest and warm, nourishing foods allow the Spleen to rebuild Qi and Blood. A calm environment prevents further Heart Blood depletion, allowing the mind to settle.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and accept help from family and friends. Eat warm, easily digested meals like congee with ginger, bone broths, and stewed fruits. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that tax the Spleen. Gentle walking and deep breathing can help rebuild Qi gradually without depleting it further.

patterns.why_this_happens:
After childbirth, emotional vulnerability and physical exhaustion easily lead to Liver Qi stagnation. When the Liver cannot keep Qi moving smoothly, it overacts on the Spleen, impairing its ability to transform fluids. This generates dampness and Phlegm, which then combine with the stagnant Qi to obstruct the chest and throat.
The result is a heavy, stuck feeling-a sensation of a lump in the throat that cannot be swallowed, chest stuffiness, and mental fog. The depression feels less like pure sadness and more like emotional dullness or being trapped, and symptoms typically worsen with stress.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal-coloured body, possibly slightly swollen, with a white greasy or slippery coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián) and slippery (滑 huá).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stress and frustration directly worsen Liver Qi stagnation, which is the engine driving Phlegm formation. Cold, raw, or greasy foods damage the Spleen, creating the dampness that turns into Phlegm, while a sedentary lifestyle allows Qi to congeal further. Gentle movement, warm meals, and emotional expression all help to move Qi, strengthen the Spleen, and transform Phlegm, gradually lifting the stuck sensation and mental fog.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals and strictly avoid cold, raw, or greasy foods, which create more dampness and Phlegm. Gentle daily walking and deep breathing exercises help move Qi and prevent stagnation. Talking through feelings with a trusted person or journaling can release pent-up emotions before they solidify into physical symptoms.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Childbirth involves significant blood loss and a sudden drop in Qi. When the body is too depleted to keep blood moving smoothly, or if cold creeps in during the postpartum period, the blood can congeal and stagnate. This is especially likely when the lochia-the normal postpartum discharge-fails to clear fully.
Stagnant blood acts like a physical blockage in the vessels. It obstructs the flow of Qi and blood to the Heart and Liver, the organs most responsible for a stable mood. The result is a heavy, stuck kind of depression that often comes with fixed, stabbing pain and a dark, dull complexion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: purple or dusky body with stasis spots; sublingual veins distended and dark. Pulse: choppy (涩 Sè), rough and uneven like a knife scraping bamboo.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood Stagnation is like a traffic jam in the vessels. Cold and stillness cause the blood to congeal further, while warmth and gentle movement get it flowing again. Emotional suppression tightens the Liver Qi, which in turn tightens the blood vessels-so letting feelings out literally eases the physical blockage. Warm foods and compresses provide the gentle heat needed to 'thaw' stagnant blood, and light exercise pumps Qi through the channels to clear the stasis.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and avoid cold, raw, or greasy meals that can congeal blood. Gentle daily walking is one of the best medicines-it keeps Qi and Blood moving without exhausting you. A warm compress on the lower abdomen can soothe stabbing pain. Do not bottle up feelings; even a short daily journal or a trusted conversation helps release the emotional tightness that feeds stagnation.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe to use while breastfeeding?
faqs.answer: Yes, when prescribed by a qualified practitioner. Chinese herbal formulas for postpartum depression are specifically chosen to be safe during breastfeeding, and many herbs actually support lactation. Always inform your practitioner that you are breastfeeding, and never self-prescribe herbs without professional guidance - some single herbs can enter breast milk and aren't suitable.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs alongside my antidepressant?
faqs.answer: It's possible, but must be done carefully and with full disclosure to both your TCM practitioner and your prescribing doctor. Some herbs can interact with SSRIs, potentially increasing serotonin levels. Your TCM practitioner will adjust the formula to avoid interactions, and your doctor can help monitor for any side effects. Never stop an antidepressant abruptly - if you want to taper, do it under medical supervision.

faqs.question: How soon after giving birth can I start acupuncture?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture can begin very soon after delivery, often within the first week, as long as there are no acute complications. It's gentle and can help with lochia discharge, perineal healing, and milk production, as well as mood. Your practitioner will avoid certain points that strongly move Blood if you are still bleeding heavily.

faqs.question: What if I don't feel better after a few weeks of herbs?
faqs.answer: It's not uncommon for the first formula to need adjustment. Postpartum patterns are dynamic - as your body recovers, the dominant imbalance may shift from, say, Blood Deficiency to Liver Stagnation. A good practitioner will reassess your tongue and pulse at each visit and modify the prescription. If you see no change after 3-4 weeks, discuss it openly; the formula likely needs refining.

faqs.question: Can diet really make a difference in postpartum mood?
faqs.answer: Yes, profoundly. In TCM, food is the foundation of postpartum recovery because it directly builds the Qi and Blood that were lost. Warm, easily digestible soups and stews with ingredients like chicken, ginger, goji berries, and red dates are far more nourishing than cold salads or raw foods. The right diet supports your herbal treatment and can noticeably improve energy and mood within a week or two.

faqs.question: Will my depression come back after I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: When treatment is stopped at the right time - after the underlying pattern is resolved and your constitution is stable - recurrence is less likely. Many practitioners continue a maintenance phase with a lower dose of herbs or monthly acupuncture for a few months after symptoms lift. The goal is to rebuild your reserves so that the normal stresses of motherhood don't tip you back into imbalance.

research.title: Meta-analysis of Xiaoyao formula as an adjuvant therapy for treating postpartum depression
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled data from multiple RCTs and found that adding Xiao Yao San to standard antidepressant therapy significantly improved clinical response rates and reduced Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores in women with postpartum depression, with a low incidence of adverse events.
research.periodical: Li X, et al. Meta-analysis of Xiaoyao formula as an adjuvant therapy for treating postpartum depression. Front Psychiatry. 2025;16:11973275.

research.title: Effect of acupuncture at thirteen ghost points on clinical efficacy and quality of life in postpartum depression
research.description: This clinical trial evaluated acupuncture at the classical thirteen ghost points for postpartum depression and found that it significantly reduced depression scores and improved quality of life measures compared to a control group, suggesting this ancient protocol is a viable non-pharmacological treatment.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Effect of acupuncture at thirteen ghost points on clinical efficacy and quality of life in postpartum depression. Zhen Ci Yan Jiu. 2021;46(9).
